lead: In the season of Denho, Paul tells us where to look for God's glory: “in the face of Jesus Christ”. In the Gospel that same face turns to a man with a withered hand, on the sabbath, in a synagogue. The glory of God and care for a suffering human being are not two subjects. Mar Thevodosios, remembered today, joined the two in his monastic life.

r.h: The light in the face of Christ
set: In 2:14–7:4 Paul defends his ministry to a Church that doubts him. He has just compared the new covenant with the old, using the veil on Moses' face (3:12–18). Now he carries the picture on: unveiled truth, the light of the gospel, and a face that shines.
str: vv. 1–2: no cunning; the open statement of the truth.
vv. 3–4: why some do not see.
vv. 5–6: not ourselves, but Christ; the light of creation shines again.
kw: Christ is “the image of God” (v. 4; see Colossians 1:15). The first human beings were made in God's image (Genesis 1:27); Christ is that image in its fullness.
In Greek, as with the Hebrew kābôd, the weight and radiance of God's presence. Moses saw it and his face shone (Exodus 34:29–35). Paul's readers see it in Christ.
Paul's word for himself in v. 5. It is the opposite of a religious leader who promotes himself.
vv: We have renounced the shameful things that one hides;
A word for preachers and teachers. There is no trick in the gospel, nor any need to bend the word to win people.
In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers,

“The god of this world” is the Evil One (compare John 12:31), and Paul is not speaking of a second god. He gives no list of who these people are. The verse teaches that the failure to see can have a cause greater than a person's own mind.
For we do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake.
“Jesus is Lord” is the Church's oldest creed (see 1 Corinthians 12:3).
it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Paul recalls Genesis 1:3. Baptism and faith are a new creation, the first day over again. Many scholars also hear an echo of Paul's own experience on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3).
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on human dignity from Christ, the image of the invisible God, in whom we see who we are (CCC 1701, citing this verse). It describes the ministry of the Church as service: those who are ordained are “slaves of Christ”, in the image of him who freely took the form of a slave for us (CCC 876).

r.h: It is lawful to do good on the sabbath
set: This is the second sabbath dispute in a row. Just before this the disciples plucked grain (12:1–8). The sabbath was a great gift to Israel, a day of rest and joy kept by God's command (Exodus 20:8–11). Jewish teachers of the time discussed in earnest what it allowed, and later rabbinic law held that saving a life overrides the sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). So this is a debate within Judaism, among people who loved the sabbath, Jesus among them.
str: vv. 9–10: the synagogue, the man and the question.
vv. 11–12: the sheep in the pit, and Jesus' teaching.
kw: The word that links both sabbath stories (12:2, 10, 12). The question is what God's Law really wants.
Literally “dried up”. The hand cannot work, and for a labouring man that may mean no bread.
so that they might accuse him
The question is asked as a test, and the man himself seems to matter little to those who ask it. Any religious person can fall into this danger.
vv: “Suppose one of you has only one sheep and it falls into a pit on the sabbath; will you not lay hold of it and lift it out?

Jesus appeals to the plain sense of his hearers. Not everyone agreed: the Qumran community's Damascus Document forbids lifting an animal from a pit on the sabbath, which shows that such cases were really discussed.
How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the sabbath.”
Jesus changes the question from “what may I not do?” to “what good can I do?”.
Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and it was restored, as sound as the other.

He does no work with his hands, not even a touch. A word, and the man's obedience. St Jerome records that a Gospel used by Jewish Christians of his time called this man a mason who begged for healing so that he need not beg for bread (in substance).
But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
Matthew speaks of those present on that day, not of all Pharisees and certainly not of the Jewish people. Nicodemus, himself a Pharisee, became a disciple in secret (CCC 595).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, gives it its authentic interpretation, and declares it a day for doing good (CCC 2173). The Christian Sunday carries on that spirit: works of mercy and care for the sick and the poor are part of keeping it (CCC 2184–2186). On the disputes of Jesus with some teachers of the Law, the Church warns against blaming the Jewish people (CCC 595–597).

rite: Today we remember Mar Thevodosios the Abbot, who built a great monastery near Bethlehem, with houses beside it for the sick, the old and the poor. Prayer and care for the suffering stood side by side, just as they do in today's readings. The man with the withered hand was healed in a house of prayer.
study: Whose face has shown me something of the glory of God?
Sunday is coming. What good could I do on the Lord's day for someone who cannot return it?
